speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the house is very well acquainted with the fact that so far as encouraging migrants to Canada is concerned, the government has laid down a very definite policy-a policy, which, I think, is very acceptable to the people of this country. On the other hand I do not think the time has come, and I hope it never will come, when the door will be closed to the admission into Canada of a British boy who comes here paying his own way and seeking to make a home for himself.
Some hon. MEMBERS Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
With respect to the boys referred to by the hon. member, for several years various organizations within the dominion, all of them, I trust, inspired with the idea that they were doing what was best for the country, have encouraged the movement of Britishers to Canada. I think at times they have been in error as to the methods they have employed, although I believe they have been acting with the very best motives.
With respect to the movement of British boys to Canada since this government took office, I have been careful to consult with all the societies concerned, who have gone to a great deal of expense down through the years to organize their efforts. I have consulted with these societies and with the provinces *with the idea of trying to determine what might be best at a time such as this. Some of the provinces said they would welcome a reduced number of boys from Great Britain, who would come out here not under assisted
Federal Loans co Provinces

passages, as in the past, but who would pay their own way and would be cared for during their first two or three years in Canada, until they could get places for themselves, by the various societies, mainly religious societies covering all religions, and in accordance with the express desire of these various organizations and of the provinces I agreed that a reduced number of boys might be admitted. If the hon. member has any fear that immigrants of this sort are likely to imperil the future of this country, I may tell him that I do not think there will be five hundred coming out this year.
I can only repeat that whatever action has been taken by the government has not been by way of extravagant encouragement; it has been taken only after careful investigation of the situation with respect to the societies concerned and the provinces which have agreed to accept these boys if they come forward.

I may not be entitled to
the information, but I did ask what guarantee if any had been given the government that these boys would not become public charges and perhaps require deportation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The very best guarantee
that could be given the government that these boys will not become public charges is that they have enough courage to come out here, paying their own way, in order to hew out homes for themselves in this dominion, and it must be remembered that they are British boys.

written me on the subject I may tell him the letter has not been received. I made some inquiry with regard to the report that good French Canadians in the constituency of Charlevoix-Saguenay, on the north shore of the river St. Lawrence, were bartering their cattle for whisky, but I could find no confirmation of that report. I can only tell my hon. friend that in the winter time, of course, the boats of the preventive service are not in operation, and I have no doubt that prohibited traffic is carried on during that time. There are some officers of the preventive service in that district, whom I have no

Unemployment Continuance Act
doubt are well known to my hon. friend. He may have assisted in having them appointed to their positions, but I have no doubt they are worthy men, and the law is being enforced on the north shore of the St. Lawrence as far as it is possible to do so. It must be remembered that this territory extends along the north shore of the St. Lawrence right to Labrador, but of the facts as stated by the hon. gentleman-and of course I must accept them-the department has no knowledge.

I did not state that
French Canadians especially were doing that bartering of goods for rum or other articles; I simply directed attention to the fact that people were coming from Newfoundland, or other places, and attempting to induce these people to go into that business. Someone suggests that they might be coming from other provinces as well.

The house resumed from Tuesday. March 15, consideration of the motion of the Prime Minister that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole on the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.

Mr. Speaker, the debate that has taken place since this resolution was introduced about three weeks ago has covered a very wide range. Almost every subject that might possibly be introduced in the House of Commons has been discussed and debated; budget speeches of last session have been rehashed; recitations have been given on a variety of subjects, and all this has been done, if we are to take the word of the Toronto Globe of March 9, in order to fulfil one purpose, that is, to carry out what the Globe refers to as the Liberal blockade.
Read it.

I have read it; if my hon. friend wants to read it for himself he can get it from the reading room. The question one is led to ask himself is, why this blockade? What is the purpose of it? To my mind it indicates the attitude of hon. members opposite towards the whole question of unemployment and farm relief. That attitude has been covered by a variety of smoke
screens, nevertheless the debate has shown the attitude of hon. members opposite towards the vital questions facing the people of this country at the present moment, unemployment and farm relief.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) gave notice of this resolution on February 22-I believe that was the date-almost immediately the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) announced that if the leader of the government and his cabinet would abdicate their functions, if they would cease to lead this house, if they would stop trying to define and introduce policies to meet the situation, then the opposition would cooperate. Their attitude was this: If you will do it our way we will cooperate; but if you come forward in your own way, after giving the matter such consideration as you have been able to devote to it, why then we will just hold the question up as long as we can. That is virtually what the leader of the opposition announced; and what has taken place in the meantime has adequately carried out that threat. The first effort they made was to throw up the smoke screen of the constitutional question in relation to this matter. At the last session of parliament we passed an act clothing the government with power to meet every situation that might arise in relation to unemployment and farm relief; or any other emergency that might occur in the difficult period through which this country, in common with the whole world, is now passing. That act automatically came to an end on March 1. On February 22 the Prime Minister announced that this resolution would be brought in, the purpose being to extend the time of the act for two months, or until May 1; and then it was that this announcement was made of cooperation or no cooperation according as the government were or were not prepared to abdicate. Not finding the going very easy in the way they had first indicated that they would take, they brought up the constitutional question; and after a variety of constitutional authorities, starting with the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), had given their judgment, the hon. member for Quebec East, the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), and my hon. friend the member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) were brought in to bolster up the position with regard to the constitution.
Now there is one thing that the house can be always sure of. When the hon. member for Quebec East rises, one of two things will happen: Either he is going to tear the British North America Act to pieces and build a new constitution, as he professes to have done

Unemployment Continuance Act
at a recent imperial conference, or he is going to throw himself in the way of someone who is anxious to destroy the constitution we have and the institutions of this country. The hon. member for Labelle takes the same position, as a rule-some constitutional question or other, something that is going to arouse passion and prejudice from one end of the country to the other. Following that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) gave us his views on the institutional-not constitutional-question. And so on and so on all through the piece. Let me assure these hon. gentlemen that the constitution and the institutions of this country are just as safe in the hands of the present Prime Minister and the present government as they have ever been or ever will be in the hands of the hon. member for Quebec East, or the hon. member for Labelle, or the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
But to come back to the question as to the way that was proposed. The leader of the opposition, in elaborating his plans, said in effect: We will call a conference and we will talk about the question. It is true there is unemployment; it is true the farmers of the west require seed wheat. Well, we will talk about it; we will call in people from every part of the dominion and talk to them about the question. We will not act; we will talk. Now, every member of this house knows that if there is anything to be done, if there is anything which it is necessary that the government or the parliament of Canada should do to meet any situation, no matter what it may be, you may always depend upon it that the leader of the opposition and those who surround him, particularly the ex-Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), who seems especially anxious, are prepared to do the talking. We all recall that last session of parliament the leader of the opposition entertained us here for a whole day and night, talking, talking all the time, after he had thrown first one and then another senatorial friend to the wolves; and after pleading with tears in his voice for consideration of his dearly beloved son who had been sent to get the money and had not covered up his tracks, he finished his speech at the end of five and three-quarter hours. I can give you another illustration of talking, particularly the talking of the exMinister of Labour and the ex-Prime Minister.
In April, 1930, my predecessor, Mr. Bowman, pleaded with the Department of Labour, through its then minister, for the people, some 412 families, living in a town in northern Ontario, who had not had an hour's work for six months. What did the then Minister of

Labour do? He went to that town and talked to these people. He talked and talked and talked, just as he talks here, not being familiar with the situation. That not being sufficient, he was followed to the same town by the leader of the opposition in a special train; and as is his wont the right hon. gentleman on that occasion talked again. He tried to persuade those people, as he tried to persuade the people throughout Canada, that there was no unemployment situation, that unemployment was merely a dream. He said to them, "Why, haven't we given you the Dunning budget? Can you not now import your hay and oats, your silk hats and walking sticks from England free of duty"? But, Mr. Speaker, it was not hay and oats nor silk hats and walking sticks that these people wanted; they wanted work.
And cut flowers.

Yes, cut flowers too;
but the people did not want cut flowers either. The situation with which this country is faced, Mr. Speaker, is one that calls not for talk but for action; and the government, through the resolution they have submitted to this house for consideration, are preparing to take action to relieve unemployment and to provide seed wheat for the farmers in western Canada who have been burned out for the past three years, and also to assist those who require assistance. But what do we get from hon. members opposite? Talk, talk, talk.
Why don't you bring in a bill to-day and have done with the discussion?

I anticipated that question from some hon. gentleman. In reply, I would ask another question. Is there any hon. member on the other side, either the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) or perhaps my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young), who is smiling so nicely, who can tell the house what kind of estimate-not a bill-would be necessary? How many acres of land in western Canada will be seeded, and how much wheat will be required to seed the land?
How much do you want?
Sit down.
How much do you want? We will give it to you.

How much do I want? That shows the intelligence of the whole discussion. The hon. member knows as well as any man in this house or in the country knows

Unemployment Continuance Act
that it. is impossible to prepare an exact estimate to meet the situation that faces us to-day.
The hon. member for East Algoma has the floor, and unless he consents to questions he must not be interrupted.

Mr. Speaker,
I rise to a point of order. I submit that the hon.. member is not debating the resolution under consideration.
Order.
The objection is not well taken.

After declaiming
against all of these institutions, after comparing conditions in Russia with the conditions in Canada, my hon. friend said:
What are we going to do? It would seem as if the government now in power, sensing somewhat the issue at stake, is determined at all costs to maintain the present system.
What institutions have we in Canada that my hon. friend would destroy? If he would be specific, then we would know exactly how 'to deal with the situation, but after the portrayal of the ideal conditions which prevail at present in Russia he accuses the government of the determination to maintain Canadian institutions.	,
I come now for just a moment to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis), who made the following statement to be found on page 982 of Hansard:
When the Minister of Railways is discussing Russia he should not forget that Russia at the present time is at war:
I agree fully with my hon. friend; Russia to-day is at war-she is at war with civilization.

Read the rest of the
sentence.

I think the hon. member is
most unfair in not reading the whole statement.

I am repeating just
exactly what the hon. member said.
No you are not.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend made his speech and I will make mine in my own way. Hon. members of &ne house can decide whether this is fair or unfair.
I say that the hon. member is right. Russia is at war-she is at war with Canada. Russian agents are in every hamlet in this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and I am not so sure that she has not agents around these parliament buildings. Whether she has or has not, every man in this country knows that Russia is at war with Canada and she is at war in her own country.

Unemployment Continuance Act

Would the hon. member
give some proof of what seems to be an absurd statement?

The hon. member for Vancouver South, who professes to know a lot about Russia, says that Russia is at war. I say that Russia is at war with Canada. It has been proven in the courts that the soviet government sent money into Canada to pay communistic organizers to disrupt this country. For what other purpose was it sent? The hon. member confesses that Russia is at war in Russia; she is at war with her own people, she is at war with every ideal which has been held sacred by men and women ever since the dawn of civilization.
The hon. member said that the kulaks, the peasant farmers, refused to cooperate in that war and consequently had to suffer as they have suffered. It will be to the eternal glory of the kulaks that they refused to cooperate. Let us try to get a picture of the cooperation for which they were asked. The communistic, red army officers came to the peasant farmer and said:	These lands upon which
you have lived, this soil you have tilled and the home you have built are no longer your own, they are ours. The things around you are no longer your own; these children are no longer your own-they are the property of the state. If you are willing to cooperate, if you are prepared to have us destroy this home and take your children away from you, if you are prepared to stand by and see your women violated, all right, you may live and we will send you to Siberia, to Archangel or to the lumber camps on the White sea w;here you can eke out an existence on raw fish and cabbage soup. If you refuse to cooperate, we will stand you up against the wall of this home you call your own and riddle your body with bullets. That is the kind of cooperation the kulak was asked to give.
My hon. friend and his mentor, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, are constantly speaking of these ideal conditions which prevail in Russia and comparing them with what they call the demoralizing conditions which prevail in Canada. Canada is the freest country under the sun. There is not a country in the wide world where the man who wants to make his way in the world has so great an opportunity as he has in Canada. I say in all sincerity and fairness to my hon. friends:	If you feel that Russia
is a much better country in which to live than Canada, why don't you go to Russia?
I believe I can say without hesitation that 
the Department of State would present no difficulties to their securing passports, and I do not believe they would have any difficulty in entering Russia. Why don't they go there if the conditions are so ideal? Is it because comrades Stalin and Kamenoff would rather they remained in Canada to take the place of Tim Buck and his associates who are now behind the walls of Kingston penitentiary. I do not know; I am simply putting that question.

If I might ask my hon.
friend a question, would he kindly tell me how far he is from the resolution?

It is quite possible
that if agitators are allowed to run loose in this country, those who would set class against class and play on the feelings of men and women who are harassed by the conditions through which we are passing, things may be done that none of us would like to see happen. But I say right now that any man or woman in these times, I care not who or where they are, who attempts to stir up strife and set class against class and play on the passions of people is not a true and good Canadian.
Every man in this country knows that we are passing through times which are difficult for humanity all over the world. Canada is in no worse a position than other countries. As a matter of fact I believe we are in a better position than any other country, and I have confidence that Canada will pull through. I have confidence in the resourcefulness and courage and faith of the Canadian people, and I believe that with sound leadership Canada will pull through better than any other country in the world. But it is sound leadership and level heads, not agitators, that the country requires to enable us to pull through. To the Prime Minister and his government I would say that every man in this house and every man in this country has some conception of the problems which the government is called upon to meet from day to day, and every one of us knows that the Prime Minister and his government are working long and tiresome days and many, many weary nights in meeting the problems and accepting the challenge that has been thrown to them as the government which the Canadian people chose in 1930 to carry on the affairs of this country. I say without any hesitation whatsoever that the best people in this country, those who have given thought to the conditions 'through which we are passing and the situation that confronts us, are behind the Prime Minister and his government,

Unemployment Continuance Act
and the government's followers in this house are one hundred per cent behind them. Go forward, I say to the Prime Minister and his government, and meet the tasks you have to meet from day to day, and let the agitators and babblers continue to agitate and babble and the talkers continue to talk.

I should like to say a few words on the resolution now before the house. At the outset I wish to say that we on this side are just as much concerned with the great problem of unemployment confronting Canada to-day as are the members on the government side, and personally let me add that I am more concerned with the affairs of Canada than with what is happening in Russia. I think we should pay more attention to the affairs of our own country, because Russia will work out her own destiny. The problem confronting the Canadian people is what is going to happen to us in this dominion of ours.
The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion), in his speech the other day, said that Canada was to-dav facing conditions worse than any she had faced before in her history, not even excepting the war. I agree entirely with that sentiment. But I would go further and say that I for one sincerely believe that even if industry and conditions in this country do come back to what we knew as normal, industry will not be able to absorb the number of men and women who are anxious and willing to work, and that fact will have to be faced more squarely in the future if we wish to put our country on a better basis.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have blamed us on this side of the house for an alleged lack of Cooperation. I suggest that the government should first show some sign that they want cooperation from this side of the house, but I have yet to see the first gesture of anything of that kind. I have sat here and listened to the discussions that have taken place, and every time suggestions were made from this side I have heard the "ha-ha" given to them by hon. gentlemen opposite. It has been reiterated both in this house and outside that we on thi3 side consistently blocked the legislation of last year although many of our members appealed time and time again to the government to introduce legislation to deal with the unemployment situation or at least to give the house an apportunity to discuss it, but it was not until the latter end of the session that the legislation was brought down. It has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite and by the Prime Minister himself
that we consistently opposed that legislation and that if there was any delay in dealing with the unemployment situation, the delay was due to the opposition in this house. I take exception to that statement, Mr. Speaker. Even the then Minister of Labour wrote to a municipality in my riding and said that the talk on this side of the house had delayed the passing of that legislation. If I have any idea of the sort of cooperation that this government expects from us it is simply a quiet acquiescence in everything they do, a desire on their part that we say nothing and do nothing at all in this house. If the positions were reversed and hon. gentlemen opposite were sitting on this side, I am wondering if the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) and the right hon. Prime Minister would not object if we had the temerity to bring down such a proposal as is now before the house, and simply say to us: Yes, go ahead; we have no opposition to offer. It takes a great stretch of the imagination, however, to imagine that.
If there has been any delay, Mr. Speaker, I claim that the delay has come from the government side of the house. The Prime Minister knows the conditions in this country far better than any other man in Canada, and he must have been aware that this act expired on the 29th of February last, and I would ask the- next hon. member on the other side who speaks to explain to me just why an item could not have been placed in the supplementary estimates to carry on the work or to pay for unemployment relief for the next two months. As a new member I should think that would have been easy to do. 1 claim that the Prime Minister is in a position toKlay to know approximately what amount will be required to take care of the situation for the next two months.
I wish to take exception, Mr. Speaker, to some of the remarks that were made yesterday by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. He said that as we in this parliament had passed the act of last year we had endorsed the principle of this legislation. I submit that that is not in accordance with the facts. Turning to Hansard of last year I find that at page 4279 the Prime Minister said:
We should not place a limitation upon the amount that may be expended, either with respect to direct relief or otherwise, because in the one instance you create the idea "Here is a fund upon which anyone may draw without work-[DOT]
There the Prime Minister was stating the reasons why we shauld give him a blank cheque. He went on:

That is the question. If you fix it at any
sum you may suggest, I repeat, you but invite the very thing that we .desire to prevent.
Further, in reply to the right hon. leader of the opposition, the Prime Minister said:
If I were less unmindful of the soundness of the criticisms that are made by the right hon. gentleman opposite as to the interference with the general principle, I would not make the observations I do. But when we make charges against the consolidated revenue fund, as we have done continuously with respect to matters mentioned last evening by the Minister of Justice, and when since confederation we have had a frank recognition by parliament that a situation might arise in which the application of the ordinary rules would no longer be possible as witness the Finance Act of the country,
And so on. Then the last paragraph is as follows:
I am compelled to do this in the public interest. But there is no reason why the date should not be limited to the first day of March which will ensure that the house must meet at least a sufficient time before that date to enable parliament to grant such further supply as may be regarded necessary in the premises.
I claim, Mr. Speaker, that if hon. members on this side did acquiesce in or help pass that act last year it was done under the assurance that legislation would be introduced on March 1, and that hon. members would be given an opportunity to discuss this matter. In my opinion the most important functions of parliament are taxation and expenditure. If these are taken away we are deprived of practically all our important rights. Municipal councils, provincial and dominion governments are seized of the fact that the imposition of taxes and expenditures of money are very important functions. The proposal now before us virtually asks us to hand over to the executive the full powers of parliament so far as the expenditure is concerned. Personally I am in favour of voting a certain sum, and I have heard no valid reason why such a sum could not have been placed in the supplementary estimates, or a bill brought in for a specific amount. There must be some reason why the Prime Minister has not yet stated his grounds for proceeding along these lines.
At the special session of 1930 we were told, when we were asked to vote for an expenditure of $20,000,000, that if we did not pass that amount speedily we would be holding up the Imperial conference. Last year legislation was introduced at the end of the session, and we were told that as parliament was about to prorogue the legislation must be passed. It is for these reasons I cannot support the proposal now before the house. Then, again, an extension of the blank cheque will

not in my opinion take care of the situation in the provinces and municipalities which have planned schedules of work and which for a period of two months or six weeks have been standing for approval. In my opinion a blank cheque does not take care of that situation.
I feel that the whole question is going to be shelved. If, as the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) has said -and I quite agree with him-conditions are worse, and to-day we are in a more unfortunate position than we were during the late war, parliament should be considering some definite plans capable of adoption. Even at the risk of sneers from hon. members opposite, I am about to make some suggestions, believing as I do that we are really face to face with conditions such as never before have been experienced. No one can tell where the end may be. The forces of the country should be coordinated, and the government should consider the conscription of wealth. That matter was under consideration during the last war, and I am sorry no such action was taken. In my humble opinion if wealth had been conscripted at that time our burden of debt would not be as severe as it is to-day. While I know that unemployment insurance will not relieve us of our difficulties, I believe it should be fully considered, in view of the fact that all the energies of our government seem to be concentrated upon the building up of manufacturing industries.
Rates of interest should at least to some extent be controlled. From one of the municipalities in the constituency I have the honour to represent I received information that only last week the rate of interest had been raised from six per cent to six and one-half per cent. The bank said the change was due to the action of the government of British Columbia in floating a loan at six per cent. For that reason bank interest was being raised to six and one-half per cent. Something should be done in that connection, Mr. Speaker, because while wages are continually going down, interest seems to be going up, and some definite action should be taken to control it. If it were at all possible I should like to see legislation whereby the municipalities and provinces could come to the federal government and obtain loans at three per cent, the rate that is now extended to banks, they in turn lending to municipalities or provinces at twice that rate.
I should like to venture an opinion regarding agriculture. One of the reasons agriculture is not progressing as it should is that the man on the land has been entirely divorced

Unemployment Continuance Act
from it. Under our old system a man could exchange his produce and live, but to-day he must have money. Without money he is absolutely tied up. In the province of British Columbia I know of barns filled with produce, but the owners cannot obtain a five cent piece for any of it, or even exchange it for other produce. Under our present capitalistic system the agriculturist is divorced from the land, and the practice under that system of putting men out on the land will in my opinion only produce more distress. Some drastic change will have to be brought about if we are successfully to further our land schemes.
At this point I should like to refer briefly to conditions in British Columbia, and to offer some suggestions concerning that province. I may be met with the remark that British Columbia is the place to discuss those matters. When we realize, however, that fifty per cent of the commitments are to be paid for by the dominion, I think I have a right to discuss provincial matters. Business men, unions of municipalities and municipal governments irrespective of party are genuinely alarmed at conditions in British Columbia. To begin with, I claim the blank cheque of last, session did not work out as the Prime Minister suggested, or would have liked to see it work out. I should like to have seen him adopt the suggestion of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) last session and appoint a commission. I believe the Prime Minister held the idea that if any definite amount had been set there would have been a rush by the provinces to avail themselves of a large share of that fund. To obviate such a rush a bill authorizing a blank cheque was put through parliament. So fai as the province of British Columbia was concerned however the opposite was the result. That province set out on a spending program the like of which had never been witnessed there before. After the passing of legislation for the blank cheque the province had every reason to believe that unlimited funds would be obtainable at Ottawa. I have before me the words of the Premier of British Columbia, as follows:
The provincial government launched its program, employed 16,000 men, built 170 camps and contracted a cost of over $50,000 a day on the definite assurance of the federal government that it would pay half the cost.
If the federal government has decided to scale down this program drastically, as reported in Ottawa, the provincial government will insist that the responsibility rests with it, not with the province.
I say if the province of British Columbia embarked on such an extensive program of
relief works they probably did so after receiving some assurance that there were unlimited funds here in Ottawa, and that all they had to do was to go ahead with the work. They probably believed that for every dollar they expended they would receive fifty cents from the federal government. I bring these matters before the house in an endeavour to show that a commission should have been appointed. Before I take my seat I shall make some suggestions as to how future relief should be handled. This is a matter which has gone beyond a mere question of parties; no one government can solve it. If conditions are as described by the Minister of Railways and Canals, if they are worse than they were during the war period, it is time we decided to appoint a commission to handle relief, so that this serious matter may be entirely free from party control or influence. In the province of British Columbia supplies were furnished through a process of patronage. I do not think any person in that province ever saw such a quantity of needless supplies purchased. Supplies of all kinds were purchased, including wheelbarrows, blankets and even Delco electric light plants. The driver who was taking out the Delco plants told me at the time I met him that that was the hundredth Delco plant he was delivering.
I have no comment to make regarding the construction camps, except to criticize the loose way in which they were conducted. For instance, men got jobs as surveyors, men whose fathers hold high government positions, and I saw four men running around the country with a car and instruments to lay out bunkhouses, although there were plenty of foremen carpenters available and on the job. To show on what a lavish scale the money was handled, in my riding not far from my -home they built two camps- a mile apart. In one camp there were thirteen or so large bunk-houses. To supply water to this camp they erected twenty feet in the air a tank of two or three thousand gallon capacity, and then they laid down the necessary piping and plumbing for hot and cold water. When the plumbing had been completed, someone asked: "Where is the water"? Although all this money had been spent they could find no water. Someone suggested that they could get water three-quarters of a, mile down the road, but after the trenches were dug a doctor came along and said: "You cannot use that water; it is unfit to drink." He was not a Liberal; he is, I believe, a strong supporter of the government. Then they set men to dig a well, but although they went down eighty-five feet they found no water. Ultimately

they had to hire a truck and bring water to the camp in barrels. Someone may say that this scandal should be threshed out in British Columbia. Well, before Mr. Jones, the provincial Minister of Finance, came down to Ottawa three and a half million dollars had been spent. If the unemployed had received the bigger portion of the money I would have little criticism to offer, but the bulk of it went in the purchase of supplies and that from favoured wholesale houses. One manufacturer told me that he sold 50,000 blankets, and it took him out of the red.

That was one good deed,
then.

If the unemployed, the needy
and destitute, had received the major portion of the money I do not think there would be very much criticism. I counted in one camp some 450 steel wheelbarrows. They had so many that a man was to be appointed to regulate their use. Ultimately orders were received from the dominion authorities that such extravagance must cease. A serious charge was laid against even a cabinet minister. The men at a camp for the unemployed were cutting wood beside the road and burning it. It seems incredible but actually coal was brought to that camp all the way from Vancouver island. But that was not the worst of this scandal. The coal car was stopped within ten or twelve miles of the camp, and the manager, who was looking after the affairs of the cabinet minister, took the job of hauling the coal the remaining twelve miles to the camp, although that coal could have been taken up the Canadian Pacific tracks right into the camp. That charge was laid against the cabinet minister right in Victoria. And it was not laid entirely by Liberals, even some Conservatives do have a conscience-yes, there are men who^have a conscience even although they are Tories.
Oh, oh.

Yes. Those Tories were so
sore about these scandalous conditions that they made that charge in Victoria against a cabinet minister. Let me give another instance to show the astounding scale on which expenditures were made. The men in one camp were doing nothing, simply marking time, yet tenders were called for cutting wood. When it was brought to the attention of the government that those unemployed men were idle, immediately the government had the notices pulled down and quietly ordered one or two carloads of coal. Yet those men had been working cutting logs and burning them

by the roadside. The only explanation given by the minister was that a coal-burning stove had been installed in the camp.
These conditions are so serious that British Columbia has reached the point where it now cannot meet its bills. The provincial government has been advised that the banks will not advance another dollar for unemployment relief. I think it is the duty of every member aware of such scandalous abuses to bring them to the attention of the federal government, so that in future there will be no chance of a repetition of such wasteful >
expenditure. In fact, as the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggested last session, a commission should be appointed to handle unemployment relief.
I omitted to mention that machinery was bought on a scale never before known in connection with relief work; close to a million dollars worth, I believe, was purchased.
At this point I should like to commend the good work of two officials of the Dominion government. I have not yet heard anything said on their behalf, and I take this opportunity to give them a word of praise. Mr. McGeough of Vancouver and Mr. Hereford of Ottawa have so far done their duty faithfully.
I think if men of like calibre had been appointed so as to take the expenditure of unemployment relief out of the hands of the provincial government there would have been no such extravagant and reckless expenditure. But with the provincial authorities it was just a case of: "Here's the pork barrel; come and get it." And believe me, everyone who could helped himself. Before leaving that question I want to say that in my humble opinion we have reached the end of an epoch; we are now entering upon a new era in the history of this country, and probably in the history of the world. Governments of to-day, as well as those interested in politics, must make up their minds as to which way they are going to travel. I believe we have reached the parting of the ways; we must either work towards a greater, a freer and a nobler democracy or we must continue in the other direction, in which the financial institutions are leading us, which ultimately will mean some form of fascism or dictatorship. If I have to choose between the two, Mr. Speaker, I will choose the free and full democracy, but that democracy cannot be brought about unless we realize certain fundamental principles. For many long years the masses of the people of Great Britain have been fighting for a political democracy, and to-day they have practically achieved that objective. To-day they have the right to elect their representatives to parliament to legislate in their own interests, but in this country so long as parliament is dominated by the hand of finance, and so long as parliament must bow down to the will of those who control our financial institutions, we are not here as free individuals. That is the reason why I made my previous statement; I do not think we have any alternative. In the past we have achieved a political democracy, but now the great masses of the people must achieve economic freedom; we must bring about what might be called an economic democracy. In other words, we must control those institutions which, to a very large extent, control parliament at this time.
What does economic freedom mean? In the first place it means that the individual must have that economic security in life to which every citizen is entitled but which every citizen does not possess at the present time. It means that the individual to-day cannot have that sense of economic freedom while economic power is vested in the hands of a
few, who use that economic power for selfish purposes. To put the matter in another way, the economic forces of the nation must be so harnessed and controlled by parliament that they will be utilized for the common good; the present practice in industry must give way to the higher conception that the forces of production and distribution are a means of satisfying human needs and human requirements. Competitive individualism must give way to the new ideal of cooperative effort, when the individual will realize that he has an interest in the state and that the state has an interest in his well being. Under private control and ownership of the means of production this is not possible; hence we must look to something else as a way out of our difficulties.
One of the main reasons for our present financial difficulties, Mr. Speaker, is that we are passing through an era of contracting capitalism. Until 1929 we were going through a period of expanding capitalism, and now the government is engaged in the thankless task-in which they have my whole-hearted sympathy-of trying to make the contracted dollar of 1932 equal the expanded dollar of 1929. I say that cannot be done. When the government can make two and two equal six they will be able to make our present contracted dollar equal the expanded dollar of 1929. Our debt is now greater because of that fact; our interest charges have increased; our fixed annual charges to-day are greater than ever before in the history of this dominion. Our income has shrunk, not because quantity production has shrunk, although that has been the case to a certain extent. Our dollars have shrunk because values have shrunk. To-day, in spite of the hardships that we have in our midst, in spite of poverty and all that poverty entails, there is more wealth in this country, more potential wealth, than there ever has been in Canada. Now I claim it ought to be the task of governments to get down and try to deal with this fundamental question. If there were a shortage of commodities in Canada, if there were any shortage of real wealth, then there might be some excuse for the suffering which there is in this country. But, as I have said, there is no shortage of either real or potential wealth and therefore there is no excuse for any poverty in our midst.
The government have been taking a good deal of credit for the fact that 334,000 people were provided with an average of twenty-three days' work during the past six months. From my seat in parliament I want to give the government full credit for all that has been accomplished in the way of providing

I think, however, that a moment's sober reflection will show that there is nothing that we in Canada have to be proud about when we find, in the midst of so much wealth, that 334,000 men were compelled to appeal to the government to help them to eke out some miserable form of existence. But allowing the government all the credit in the world for what they have done in this respect, I want to show something of the other side of the ledger. Let us try to get a true picture of the unemployment situation in Canada.
I figure that if the amount of time worked by these men who were employed on government relief works were put upon the basis of one year's employment, it would represent employment for approximately 25,000 people. That is another way of putting it; that is to say, the government found work for 25,000 people for twelve months. Now in this year's estimates we find, out of controllable government expenditures, there is $55,000,000 less provided than was provided the year before, and I venture to say that, with the reduction in the estimates of civil government for the past fiscal year, they put as .many people out of work as they actually employed by giving an average of twenty-two dlays' work to
334.000	people.
Let us take the latest figures for the railways-because after all this is a fair barometer of conditions in Canada. I find that at the peak of 1929 there were 201,060 men employed on the railways. On December 31, 1931, a little over two months ago, there were 130,802 persons employed on the railways, a reduction of 70,258, or, in other words, a reduction of approximately thirty-five per cent in the number of men employed on the railways in Canada. And if that is the situation with regard to the railways, then I believe it is only a fair indication of what is taking place also in other industrial enterprises in Canada.
I claim that within the confines of the existing structure the government will not be in a position to find any remedies for the unemployment situation. The government have asked us for suggestions. Well, we have made many suggestions to them from this comer of the house, but they take our suggestions and throw them into the waste basket, and therefore we . do not feel inclined to offer many more. We do not want to have our suggestions handled in such an unceremonious manner. But we have put forward suggestions.

For example, seven years ago the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and I offered a suggestion with regard to old age .pensions, and we were likened to Robin Hood because we dared to ask for some provision for the aged. Then we made a request for unemployment insurance, and although we were told five or six years ago that we were rather premature in putting forward that suggestion, we find that to-day all hon. members are in favour of granting some form of unemployment insurance. I sincerely trust that during the lifetime of this parliament the government will introduce a measure of unemployment insurance and that it will be of such a nature that we of the Labour group can support it. Again, a few weeks ago we suggested shorter hours and increased purchasing power. But all these have gone into the discard as not acceptable.
Now I am going to offer one other suggestion, a novel one perhaps, but one that has been discussed for many years; and in view of the fact that the unemployed portion of our population seems to be something more or less permanent in the social structure of the country, and although the present government or any government in the immediate future may not be able or willing to handle it fundamentally, I should like to see the government seriously consider the proposal of trying to make the unemployed in Canada a self-contained element in the community. I know that a proposal of that sort could be discussed pro and con and a good deal could be said against it as for it. But after giving this question a little study I believe that, while all that could be said against it would have considerable weight with those who might form an opinion, the idea of making the unemployed in this country self-sustained, so that they might be able to retain all that is best in them, is something that is worthy of serious consideration both by the government and by members of this house.
Before I conclude I wish to refer to some remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), remarks which I do not think ought to go unchallenged in this house. I have a good deal of respect for any hon. gentleman elected as a member of this house. A good deal of honour attaches to any man who has the confidence of the people who elect him to represent them in this chamber, and there is always in this house a certain standard of conduct which I believe most hon. members try honestly to observe. When the hon. member for East Algoma spoke this afternoon he discussed certain observations made by my
